column2: Expose believable network-facing printer services that an adversary can discover and interact with.
Core Stage 1 architecture plus relevant supporting exposure components: Web UI, REST API, WebSocket, Telnet, Other Services, Firmware Identity, Printer Profile, and Access Logging.
Adversary → Exposed Network Interfaces → Host / Management Segment

column4: Implementation Approach: existing software, extend existing, or build new?

column3: I mapped Web UI to Stage 3 > Software > Build-execution software / HMI because it is the operator-facing interface used to view printer status, control jobs, and interact with the machine during build execution.
column4: Extend OctoPrint-like web behavior with a custom HoneyPrint interface. (Python (aiohttp + aiohttp-jinja2 + Jinja2))
column5: Present a realistic browser-accessible printer-management surface for reconnaissance and interaction.
column6: HTTP/HTTPS pages and management views that expose believable printer identity, status, and controls.

column2: Stage 3 > Software > Build-execution software / HMI; Stage 2 > Network > Transfer to printer network
column3: I mapped REST API to Stage 3 > Software > Build-execution software / HMI and Stage 2 > Network > Transfer to printer network because the API exposes printer/job management functions and also carries file-transfer operations into the printer workflow.
column4: Extend OctoPrint/Moonraker-style API semantics with custom HoneyPrint JSON handlers. (Python (aiohttp + json + asyncio))
column5: Provide programmatic printer-management endpoints for status queries, files, jobs, and commands.
column6: Structured JSON request/response behavior tied to the shared simulated printer state.

column2: Stage 3 > Software > In-situ monitoring & analytics; Stage 3 > Network > Monitoring & logging channels
column3: I mapped WebSocket to Stage 3 > Software > In-situ monitoring & analytics and Stage 3 > Network > Monitoring & logging channels because it streams live machine, job, and sensor state while also carrying real-time operational events over the network.
column4: Reuse WebSocket transport and build a custom HoneyPrint real-time telemetry publisher. (Python (aiohttp WebSocketResponse + asyncio + json))
column5: Stream live printer, job, and sensor state so exposed services do not appear static.
column6: Continuous real-time telemetry reflecting changes in the simulator and active interactions.

column2: Stage 3 > Network > Ethernet / Wi-Fi / USB links; Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control
column3: I mapped Telnet to Stage 3 > Network > Ethernet / Wi-Fi / USB links and Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control because Telnet provides the network transport while the session directly exchanges firmware-style G-code commands and responses.
column4: Reuse Telnet transport and bridge it to the custom HoneyPrint firmware emulator. (Python (asyncio + telnetlib3))
column5: Expose a direct firmware-style console independent of the web-management layer.
column6: Interactive low-level command/response sessions using the simulated firmware state.

column3: I mapped Other Services to Stage 3 > Network > OT / industrial network because optional services such as SSH or MQTT represent additional operational-network entry points around the printer environment.
column4: Keep optional network-service adapters configurable and expose only services implemented by the selected HoneyPrint profile. (Python (asyncio + PyYAML + service adapters))
column5: Allow the exposed network personality to include additional believable printer-related services when configured.
column6: Profile-controlled optional service exposure without changing the underlying simulated printer state.

column2: Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control
column3: I mapped Firmware Identity to Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control because version, capability, and firmware-identification responses are generated by the emulated firmware layer.
column4: Reuse Marlin/Klipper identity semantics and implement profile-aware HoneyPrint identity responses. (Python (re + dataclasses + PyYAML))
column5: Return believable firmware version, capability, and identity information during reconnaissance.
column6: Profile-consistent firmware identity and capability responses such as Marlin-style identification output.

column2: Stage 3 > Hardware > AM machine / 3D printer; Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control
column3: I mapped Printer Profile to Stage 3 > Hardware > AM machine / 3D printer and Stage 3 > Software > Printer firmware & motion control because the profile defines machine-specific physical limits and identity while also controlling firmware-facing capabilities and responses.
column4: Extend custom HoneyPrint personality profiles and reuse YAML/configuration loading. (Python (PyYAML + pydantic + dataclasses))
column5: Let one deployment present different printer models, limits, capabilities, and firmware-facing characteristics.
column6: Model-specific identity, dimensions, limits, and selected behavior exposed consistently across services.

column3: I mapped Access Logging to Stage 3 > Network > Monitoring & logging channels because it records source addresses, requests, endpoints, and service-access events generated through network interactions.
column4: Build custom request/event capture and reuse HTTP/Telnet metadata where available. (Python (aiohttp middleware + logging + datetime + structlog))
column5: Capture reconnaissance and service-access activity from the first interaction.
column6: Timestamped access events including source, service, endpoint/action, and basic client metadata.
